hook: Rome's greatest general before Caesar, and Caesar's partner, then rival.

pages.x: Gnaeus Pompeius was born in 106 BC to a rich family. At 23 he raised his own army to fight for the dictator Sulla, and won so many victories in Sicily and Africa that Sulla, half joking, called him Magnus: "the Great". He held a triumph before he was even a senator.

In 67 BC pirates ruled the Mediterranean, kidnapping nobles and cutting off the grain that fed Rome. Given command of the whole sea, Pompey divided it into 13 zones and swept it clean in about three months.

He then beat Mithridates of Pontus, Rome's most stubborn enemy, and reorganised the East. Syria became a Roman province, and in 63 BC he took Jerusalem and walked into the Holy of Holies of the Temple, where only the high priest was allowed.

In 60 BC he joined Caesar and Crassus in a secret pact to run Rome, and married Caesar's daughter, Julia. He built Rome's first stone theatre. When Julia died in 54 BC and Crassus was killed in battle a year later, the two great men drifted apart.

When Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, Pompey fled to Greece to raise an army. At Pharsalus in 48 BC his larger army was routed. He sailed to Egypt for help, but the advisers of its boy king, hoping to please Caesar, had him stabbed to death as he stepped ashore.

When Caesar reached Egypt a few days later, he was handed Pompey's head and his signet ring. He turned away and wept. Whether his tears were real, no one could say, but he had the ashes sent home to Pompey's widow.
Pompey stretched Rome's power across the East, making Syria and Judea Roman. His rivalry with Caesar tore the Republic apart and opened the way for the emperors.
pts: Won fame as a general while still a young man
Swept the pirates from the Mediterranean
Made Syria and Judea part of Rome
